keep mind occupied all the time

Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again

When I remember the event I feel intense rage

issues.item: Triggers: Power Imbalance: Being in a situation where someone has power over me
issues.explanation: The trigger 'being in a situation where someone has power over me' is hard to reconcile with the stated trauma type of natural disaster and with the rest of the profile, which otherwise emphasizes alarm/reactivity and fragmented recall rather than interpersonal domination or coercion. For this trauma type, this item introduces an implausible trigger theme not supported elsewhere in threat, memory, or appraisals.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
issues.explanation: Avoiding hospitals/ambulances/physical examinations is not well supported by the rest of the profile for a natural-disaster trauma. There are no memory or threat items involving injury treatment, medical rescue, or bodily harm, so this strategy appears to target a symptom theme not represented elsewhere. In contrast, the profile is centered on generalized alarm, shouting, unpredictability, and fragmented memory.

issues.item: Self-Harm: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings
issues.explanation: Self-harm is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile and trauma context: the other selected items describe a classic hyperarousal/re-experiencing natural-disaster PTSD presentation with avoidance and overeating, but no accompanying items suggest the kind of shame, self-punitive appraisal, dissociative affect regulation, or broader emotion-dysregulation pattern that would make physical self-harm clinically coherent here. It stands out as addressing a symptom process not otherwise represented in the five components.

Alcohol smell is not impossible, but in this profile it is weakly anchored to the reported trauma type and the rest of the item set. The other triggers (unpredictability, shouting) fit a danger/hyperarousal formulation, whereas alcohol smell implies a very specific sensory trauma cue that is not supported by the memory or threat items. Given a natural-disaster index trauma, this trigger is difficult to explain clinically without additional corroborating content.

vignette: Kofi had always been a man who thrived in high-pressure situations. As a bomb disposal technician, he had spent years honing his skills to stay calm and focused in the face of danger. But it was not an explosion that shattered his sense of control, but a hurricane that ravaged his hometown five years ago. Kofi's family had been lucky to escape with their lives, but the experience left him shaken. He remembered the sound of the wind howling like a chorus of banshees, the walls creaking and groaning as if they would collapse at any moment, and the feeling of utter powerlessness as he huddled with his wife and children in the basement, praying for it to pass. The storm's unpredictability had been terrifying - one minute the winds were calm, the next they were raging like a beast unleashed. In the aftermath of the hurricane, Kofi began to notice that loud noises made him jump. At first, it was just the sound of thunder or a car backfiring, but soon he found himself flinching at any sudden noise - a slammed door, a shout from his child, even the beeping of the microwave. His wife would try to reassure him, but Kofi couldn't shake off the feeling that disaster was lurking around every corner. To manage his growing anxiety, Kofi turned to food. He started eating more and more, using the comfort of familiar tastes and textures to calm his racing mind. His weight began to balloon, and his wife expressed concern, but Kofi just shrugged it off. It was easier to eat than to confront the memories that lurked in the shadows of his mind. As time passed, Kofi became increasingly adept at avoiding anything that might trigger those memories. He stopped going to crowded places, avoided loud events, and even quit his beloved hobby of woodworking because the sound of the power tools was too much for him to bear. His work as a bomb disposal technician began to suffer - he found himself hesitating in situations where he once would have acted with confidence. But despite his best efforts, Kofi's body seemed to react before his mind could catch up. He would find himself sweating and trembling at the slightest provocation, his heart racing like a jackrabbit on steroids. Sometimes, he would even experience flashbacks - sudden, jarring moments where he was transported back to that basement, reliving the terror of the hurricane. When Kofi tried to recall the event, he found himself pushing the memories away before they could fully form. It was as if his mind was trying to protect him from the pain and fear by fragmenting the recollection into disjointed images and sounds. But when he did manage to piece together fragments of that day, a wave of intense rage would wash over him, leaving him feeling shaken and guilty. Lately, Kofi's wife had been noticing changes in his behavior - the way he flinched at every loud noise, the way he avoided social gatherings, the way he seemed to be constantly on edge. She encouraged him to seek help, but Kofi was hesitant - what if therapy couldn't fix him? What if he was forever trapped in this cycle of fear and avoidance? It wasn't until his boss expressed concern about his performance at work that Kofi realized he needed to confront his demons head-on. He made the difficult decision to seek help, hoping against hope that a therapist could guide him through the treacherous landscape of his own mind and back into the life he once knew. As he sat in the waiting room, clutching his worn copy of the PTSD support group pamphlet, Kofi felt a glimmer of determination - maybe, just maybe, he could learn to face the storm within himself.
